blocks.text: Amy Stanford Gaskin is a Los Angeles–based photographer and journalist known for her ability to gain extraordinary access to the people she photographs. By spending time with those who welcome her into their worlds, she creates images that capture the humanity, authenticity, and truth at the heart of her work. Her photography and journalism have been featured in National Geographic, Stern Magazine, The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, and The Guardian , among other publications.

Her new book, Marilyn Forever! Marilyn Monroe—A Symbol of Hope (Roche Publishing), explores the deeply personal and often unexpected ways Marilyn Monroe continues to inspire people around the world—far beyond her enduring fame and Hollywood stardom. The book was selected by People magazine as one of its Top 10 books about Marilyn Monroe, earning the #3 spot
Staley-Wise Gallery in New York City is currently exhibiting selected images from the Marilyn series and represents the project.

Gaskin’s honors include being named a finalist for the World Report Award; five National wins in the Best of ASMP competition presented by the American Society of Media Photographers; four National wins from American Photographic Artists (APA); First Place in the International Color Awards; recognition from the Lucie Foundation (MOPLA) and the International Photography Awards; and honors from the Leica and Fujifilm awards at the Palm Springs Photo Festival. She was also named a Top 50 winner in Critical Mass.

The Festival of Ethical Photography in Lodi, Italy, produced a large exhibition of her work. Her images have been selected for group shows by jurors from major museums and photographic organizations around the world, including the J. Paul Getty Museum; National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC; Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; Groninger Museum, Netherlands, Los Angeles County Museum of Art; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; among others. Her horse racing images are part of the permanent collection of the National Museum of Racing and Hall of Fame.

She is President Emerita of the Press Photographers Association of Greater Los Angeles, a 90-year-old organization representing more than 400 members of the broadcast and still-image news media throughout the Greater Los Angeles area. In 2024, she was inducted into the Council of One Hundred at Northwestern University, an organization recognizing 100 distinguished living female graduates of the university.

Patricia Lanza : Marilyn is one of the most photographed people in history. How did you come to make or discover something visually new about someone whose image already seems completely known?

Amy Gaskin : I didn’t know much about Marilyn when I happened to find the lipstick kisses on her grave during the heart of the pandemic. This was during the time when we were afraid to touch our groceries, so the idea of kisses on the grave seemed especially unusual. I’m a naturally curious person and I genuinely wanted to know why people were visiting this crypt. This cemetery has many other stars’ graves, but I didn’t see any lipstick on those. Upon interviewing the visitors to Marilyn’s crypt, I became interested in them right away as their stories were very personal. I listened to how Marilyn inspires them directly, in their lives. Virtually everyone I met was relating to who she was as a person, rather than her stardom. I had never heard this angle before.

Marilyn’s background of overcoming so many challenges inspires people. She had a very difficult childhood and upbringing. She spent time in foster care and in an orphanage not far from a famous Hollywood studio which she could see from her room. At night, she would cry, dreaming of becoming a star. She more than achieved that dream, as we know. She was one of the early women in Hollywood to have her own production company, yet she routinely had her intelligence underestimated. She was inclusive of all kinds of people which is a big reason many relate to her. Many who feel disenfranchised shared examples of Marilyn’s kindness and inclusivity of all types.

The people on the cover of my book are not look-alikes. Instead, they see her as a symbol of hope for cancer and dress as her each year to raise money for cancer research in Australia. Marilyn as a personal inspiration is something that is a worldwide phenomenon.
The scope of her Marilyn’s reach and embodiment of hope is mind-boggling.
Patricia Lanza : As a photojournalist, how did your background shape the way you photographed, and researched this series. What were you looking for evidence, symbolism, intimacy or something else?

Amy Gaskin : I allowed the picture of Marilyn to be created by those remembering her today. I didn’t set out with an agenda, nor did I know much about her beforehand, which I think was helpful. I was looking for the truth about the memory of Marilyn. When we die, what do we leave behind? What matters about how we lived? How are we remembered by the world? How does someone inspire others?

The book is a portrait of Marilyn — like a mosaic of her told through first-hand accounts of people who are inspired by her and, in some cases, knew her personally. By using first-hand accounts and then researching what they told me about her personal story, I made every effort to ensure that what is presented as a fact about Marilyn is indeed true.

The painstaking methodology preserved the authenticity. Everything in the book somehow has origins at the crypt. By finding people there and following leads from there, I could be sure that the people I interacted with truly do feel a connection to Marilyn — as opposed to simply placing an ad for volunteers.
Ultimately, I believe that the subject of Marilyn’s legacy becomes a catalyst for a larger conversation about what really matters in life.
Patricia Lanza : The “personal stories” create an in-depth account 60+years after her death. What were some of the most surprising revelations?
Amy Gaskin : There was a woman named Donna who has tattooed Marilyn over her heart and has purchased the nearest crypt she could to Marilyn’s, even though her family lives in the United Kingdom.

Donna explained, “I was the black sheep of the family. I felt different, but I didn’t know why until I got older. When I first came out, my mom didn’t speak to me for a year. She was born the same year as Marilyn, but they were very different in their views.”

“Marilyn is very relatable, with what she went through and what she achieved. She stuck up for human rights and didn’t like racism. She wasn’t afraid to say what she felt. I wanted to be like that. Through her actions and acceptance of all types of people, he was trying to say, ‘Love is love. It doesn’t matter your color, your sexuality, or anything like that.’ She was very much ahead of her time.”

Some of the most profound revelations were Marilyn’s influences across so many seemingly different backgrounds. What shines through is her humanity. They feel she is relatable because she went through many of the same things that people today continue to experience. Upon finding the interview where jazz singer Ella Fitzgerald said, “I owe Marilyn a real debt. She was an unusual woman — a little ahead of her time. And she didn’t know it,” I found this incredible.

So much of what Marilyn did at the time, she may have not thought was remarkable. For instance, seeking out children who are Black to be photographed with in an orphanage. Being friends with people who were openly gay. It is important to remember that these acts of kindness were during a short life which ended in 1962. When we look at the period of the 1950s – 60s, we see that Marilyn chose to be inclusive, when others were not. So many people told me she was ahead of her time.

Patricia Lanza : A monograph is a very different experience from seeing individual photographs online or in an exhibition. What did the physical book allow you to do that another format couldn’t? If Marilyn could see this book, what would you hope she recognized in it?

Amy Gaskin : I see the book as a mosaic or tapestry of many encounters with people today who, collectively, paint the picture of Marilyn’s true legacy. The physical book allowed me to paint the complete image of what I had learned from them about Marilyn. There are so many facets uncovered that the full picture cannot be seen in the space of an article, for instance. Each person included here represents literally hundreds more whom I interviewed.

If Marilyn were to see this book, I think she would be astonished. People are remembering her for her humanity — rather than her stardom. She is being celebrated worldwide for things she did in her life that seemed to come naturally for her.

The book is about much more than Marilyn. Marilyn is a catalyst here for a larger conversation about what really matters in life. Who are we and how do we treat each other? Are we inclusive and kind? How do we persevere and overcome the challenges in our lives? How do we find hope and inspiration?
Patricia Lanza : What are you looking to do now that the book is published and the exhibition was produced at the Lodi, Italy photographic festival this year?

Amy Gaskin : The festival in Lodi was a wonderful place to share these ideas of hope, inclusivity, and doing more than we dreamed possible in life. I plan to continue speaking and sharing the work and message wherever I can. The book is a catalyst for conversation about what matters most in life.
Please don’t hesitate to contact me to continue the conversation!
Text and interview by Patricia Lanza
